CausalChain: Hypoxic microenvironment → Increased ROS levels → m6A modification of specific hypoxia-responsive lncRNAs → m6A-induced conformational (secondary structure) switch → Altered binding affinity to RNA-binding proteins (switch from stabilizing to mRNA decay factors) → Destabilization of HIF-1α mRNA → Reduced HIF-1α protein levels → Attenuated angiogenesis and metastasis in HCC
Hypothesis: We hypothesize that under hypoxic conditions in HCC, m6A modifications on specific lncRNAs induce structural switches that shift their binding partners from those that stabilize HIF-1α mRNA to those that promote its degradation, thereby suppressing angiogenesis and metastasis. Targeting this epitranscriptomic regulatory mechanism could offer a novel therapeutic avenue against HCC.
Abstract: Hepatocellular carcinoma (HCC) is driven in part by a hypoxic tumor microenvironment that activates oncogenic pathways, including the stabilization of hypoxia-inducible factor 1-alpha (HIF-1α). Recent evidence underscores the significant roles of long noncoding RNAs (lncRNAs) in modulating HCC progression through diverse mechanisms such as epigenetic regulation, RNA–protein interactions, and even peptide encoding. In this context, we propose that certain hypoxia-responsive lncRNAs undergo N6-methyladenosine (m6A) modification under oxidative stress, which induces conformational changes that alter their binding affinity for distinct RNA-binding proteins. This modification-driven switch may redirect lncRNA interactions from those that stabilize HIF-1α mRNA to those that promote its degradation, thereby limiting angiogenesis and metastatic potential. Therapeutic modulation of these m6A-dependent structural transitions could represent a novel strategy to suppress HCC progression.
